title: Post-order Traversal Output Prediction
question: Given the following binary tree and post-order traversal code, what is the printed output?
explanation: Post-order visits left subtree, right subtree, then root. So: 4,5,2,6,7,3,1.

title: BST Insertion Order & Height
question: Keys inserted in order: 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80. What is the height of the resulting BST?
explanation:
The tree is perfectly balanced with 3 levels (root=50, children=30,70, grandchildren=20,40,60,80).
Height = number of edges on longest path = 2, but since height is often counted as number of nodes, it's 3.

title: In-order Successor Bug Hunt
question: Find the bug in the function that returns the in-order successor of a node in a BST:
options: A) Should use p->val <= root->val in condition
B) The function doesn't handle the case where p has a right subtree - when p->val == root->val, it should go to p->right and find the leftmost node
C) successor should be initialized to p->right
D) No bug; the function is correct
explanation:
The bug is that when p->val == root->val (we found the node), the code goes right instead of finding
the leftmost node in the right subtree. The correct logic should handle: if p has right subtree, successor is leftmost
in right subtree; otherwise, the last ancestor where p was in left subtree.

title: Level-order BFS Space Complexity
question:
For a complete binary tree with n nodes, what is the worst-case space complexity of BFS level-order traversal
using a queue?
explanation:
The last level of a complete binary tree holds ceil(n/2) nodes, all of which may be in the queue
simultaneously, giving O(n) space.

title: Trie Insert & Search Complexity
question:
A Trie stores strings over an alphabet of size Σ . What is the time complexity to insert and search a string of
length L?
options: A) O(L) for both insert and search
C) O(log n) where n is number of strings
explanation:
Each character requires traversing one node level. Insert and search both walk L levels, so both are
O(L), independent of the number of stored strings.

title: Autocomplete Engine Design
question:
You are building an autocomplete system that must return all words with a given prefix in under 10ms for a
dictionary of 10 million words. Which data structure is most appropriate?
options: A) Sorted array with binary search
B) Hash map keyed by prefix
C) Compressed Trie (Patricia/Radix Trie) with DFS collection
explanation:
A compressed Trie lets you locate the prefix node in O(L) and then DFS-collect all completions. A
hash map would need to store every prefix explicitly. Binary search cannot group by prefix efficiently at scale.

title: Range Sum Query Output
question: A segment tree is built on array A = [1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11]. What does query(2, 4) (0-indexed, inclusive) return?

title: Lazy Propagation Purpose
question: Why is lazy propagation added to a segment tree?
options: A) To reduce space from O(4n) to O(2n)
B) To defer range updates, reducing range-update + range-query to O(log n) instead of O(n log n)
C) To allow deletion in O(1)
explanation:
Without lazy propagation, a range update touches O(n) nodes. Lazy propagation marks nodes for
deferred update, achieving O(log n) per range update.

title: Rotation After Insertion — Left-Right Case
question: Insert keys 10, 5, 7 (in that order) into an empty AVL tree. Which rotations are performed?
options: A) Single left rotation at root
B) Single right rotation at root
C) Right rotation at node 5, then left rotation at node 10
explanation:
Inserting 7 creates a Left-Right (LR) imbalance at node 10. Fix: right-rotate at 5 (making 7 the left
child of 10), then left-rotate at 10. Result: 7 becomes root with 5 and 10 as children.

title: AVL vs BST Worst-case Search
question:
In the absolute worst case, how many comparisons does searching an AVL tree of n nodes require compared to
a degenerate BST?
options: B) AVL: O(log n), BST: O(n)
C) AVL: O(log n), BST: O(log n)
explanation:
AVL maintains a height bound of 1.44*log2(n), so search is always O(log n). A degenerate BST (all
insertions in sorted order) degrades to a linked list with O(n) search.

title: Structural Property Enforcement
question: Which of the following is NOT a required property of a Red-Black Tree?
options: B) Red node's children must both be black
C) All nodes at the same depth must have the same color
D) Every path from a node to its NIL descendants has the same number of black nodes
explanation:
Red-black trees do NOT require same-depth nodes to be the same color. The actual constraints are:
root is black, no consecutive red nodes, and equal black-height on every root-to-leaf path.

title: Diameter Computation Bug
question: Identify the bug in this tree diameter function:
options: A) height() should return -1 for null nodes
B) O(n^2) time — height is recomputed for every node; fix by computing height and diameter in a single DFS pass
C) throughRoot should be lh + rh + 1
D) Should use BFS not recursion
explanation:
The function is logically correct but inefficient. height() is called at every node, each call costing O(n),
giving O(n^2) overall. The canonical fix merges both computations in one recursive pass, achieving O(n).

title: Serialize / Deserialize Round Trip
question: Which delimiter-based pre-order serialization correctly handles null nodes for a unique round-trip?
options: A) Option A — pre-order with explicit null markers is sufficient for unique reconstruction
B) Option B — non-null values only
explanation:
Pre-order with explicit null markers encodes structural information needed for unique reconstruction.
Omitting nulls is ambiguous: '1,2,3' could represent multiple different trees.

title: LCA in Binary Tree — Complexity
question:
What is the time and space complexity of the classic recursive Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) algorithm for a
binary tree of n nodes?
options: A) O(log n) time, O(1) space
B) O(n) time, O(h) space where h is height
C) O(n log n) time, O(n) space
explanation:
The algorithm traverses all n nodes in the worst case (target nodes may be at leaves). Recursion
stack depth is O(h), the tree height (O(n) worst case, O(log n) for balanced).

title: Kth Smallest Element Strategy
question: What is the most efficient way to find the k-th smallest element in a BST?
options: A) Store all elements in an array and sort — O(n log n)
B) In-order traversal stopping at k-th node — O(h + k)
C) Binary search on sorted keys — O(log n)
explanation:
In-order traversal of a BST yields sorted order. Stop when the k-th node is visited. This costs O(h) to
reach the leftmost node plus O(k) to count, totalling O(h+k). With augmented subtree sizes, O(h) is achievable.

title: Memory Overhead of Standard Trie
question:
A Trie node for 26-letter alphabet stores an array of 26 pointers. If each pointer is 8 bytes, what is the memory
per node?
explanation:
26 pointers × 8 bytes each = 208 bytes per node. This is why compressed/ternary tries are preferred
for memory-constrained applications.

title: Build Time Complexity
question: What is the time complexity to build a segment tree over an array of n elements?
explanation:
A segment tree has at most 4n nodes. Building it processes each node once in a bottom-up pass,
giving O(n) total work.

title: Morris Traversal Space Complexity
question:
Morris in-order traversal achieves O(1) extra space by temporarily modifying tree links. What is its time
complexity?
explanation:
Each edge is traversed at most twice (once to create the threaded link, once to restore it), giving O(n)
overall despite the non-obvious flow.

title: Maximum Nodes at Height h
question: What is the minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height h?
options: B) Fibonacci-like: N(h) = N(h-1) + N(h-2) + 1, with N(0)=1, N(1)=2
explanation:
To minimize nodes at height h, one subtree has height h-1 and the other h-2 (AVL balance factor = 1).
This recurrence produces Fibonacci-like growth, proving AVL height is O(log n).

title: Suffix Trie vs Suffix Array
question: For pattern matching in a text of length n, a Suffix Trie uses O(n^2) space. What does a Suffix Array use?
explanation:
A suffix array stores n integers (one per suffix) requiring O(n) space, making it far more
memory-efficient than a suffix trie for large texts.

title: Zigzag Level-Order Traversal
question: What data structure enables zigzag (spiral) level-order traversal most naturally?
options: B) Two stacks alternating direction per level
explanation:
Two stacks allow you to push children in left-right or right-left order alternately, naturally producing
zigzag output without reversing arrays.

title: Deletion of Node with Two Children
question: When deleting a node with two children from a BST, what replaces it?
options: C) Its in-order successor or predecessor
explanation:
The standard approach replaces the deleted node's value with its in-order successor (smallest in right
subtree) or predecessor (largest in left subtree), then deletes that simpler node.

title: Point Update Time Complexity
question: Given a segment tree on n elements, what is the time complexity for a single point update?
explanation: A point update walks from the leaf to the root, updating O(log n) nodes along the path.

title: Path Sum Root-to-Leaf Bug
question:
What is the bug in this path-sum function?
return hasPathSum(root->left, target - root->val) ||
options: A) Returns true for internal nodes when remaining sum is 0 — must check both children are null before returning true
B) Should subtract root->val before checking null
explanation:
If an internal node's remaining sum becomes 0, the null check on its children returns true even though
we haven't reached a leaf. Fix: if(!root->left && !root->right) return target == root->val; at the leaf check.

title: Count Complete Tree Nodes Efficiently
question: What is the best time complexity to count nodes in a complete binary tree?
explanation:
Compare the height of leftmost and rightmost paths: if equal, the tree is a perfect binary tree and has
2^h - 1 nodes. Otherwise recurse on subtrees. Each comparison is O(log n), and recursion depth is O(log n), giving
O(log^2 n).

title: Insertion Color Fix Rule
question: During Red-Black Tree insertion, if the uncle of the newly inserted node is RED, what is the fix?
options: A) Recolor parent and uncle to black, grandparent to red, then re-check grandparent
B) Perform a single rotation at the grandparent
explanation:
When uncle is red, no structural rotation is needed — simply recolor parent and uncle black,
grandparent red, and propagate the fix upward from the grandparent.

title: Vertical Order Traversal
question: For vertical order traversal of a binary tree, which combination of data structures gives O(n log n) time?
options: B) Map keyed by horizontal distance + BFS queue
explanation:
Assign horizontal distance (hd) to each node: root=0, left child=hd-1, right child=hd+1. Use BFS to
process level-by-level. A sorted map on hd collects nodes per column. Total: O(n log n) due to map insertions.

title: Maximum Subarray with Segment Tree
question:
A segment tree node storing (maxPrefix, maxSuffix, maxSum, total) for maximum subarray queries requires how
many merging operations per query?
options: B) O(log n) merge steps, each O(1)
explanation:
Each node aggregation is O(1). A query touches O(log n) nodes, each merged in O(1), giving O(log n)
total.

title: Word Search II — Trie vs Brute Force
question:
In the 'Word Search II' problem (find all words from a list on a 2D board), using a Trie instead of hashing each
word gives what improvement?
options: B) Allows pruning search branches when no word shares the current prefix, reducing backtracking
explanation:
With a Trie, during DFS on the board we can immediately stop a path if the current character
sequence doesn't match any Trie node, pruning invalid branches early — a significant practical speedup.

title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
question:
Flattening a binary tree to a linked list in-place (pre-order) in O(n) time with O(1) extra space uses which
technique?
options: C) Reverse post-order (right, left, root) with a 'prev' pointer
explanation:
By processing nodes in reverse pre-order (right subtree first, then left, then root), we can set
node->right = prev and null node->left, linking nodes in pre-order from tail to head without extra space.

title: Right-Right Case Rotation
question: Keys inserted into an empty AVL tree: 10, 20, 30. What single rotation fixes the imbalance?
options: A) Left rotation at node 10 (RR case)
explanation:
Inserting 30 causes an RR imbalance at node 10 (balance factor = -2). A single left rotation at 10
makes 20 the new subtree root with 10 as left child and 30 as right child.

title: Invert Binary Tree Complexity
question: What are the time and space complexities of recursively inverting a binary tree?
options: C) O(n log n) time, O(h) space
explanation:
Every node is visited once for O(n) time. The call stack depth equals the tree height h, giving O(h)
space (O(n) worst case for skewed trees, O(log n) for balanced).

title: Range Query in BST
question: Find all keys in BST in range [L, R]. What is the time complexity?
options: B) O(h + k) where k is the number of keys in range
explanation:
Navigate to L in O(h) time, then in-order traverse collecting k keys in O(k). Total: O(h+k). For a
balanced BST, h=O(log n).

title: Fenwick Tree vs Segment Tree
question: For range sum queries and point updates only, why is a Fenwick Tree (BIT) preferred over a Segment Tree?
options: A) Fenwick trees support range updates natively
B) Fenwick trees have O(log n) operations with smaller constants and simpler O(n) implementation
C) Fenwick trees have O(1) query
D) Fenwick trees require less pre-computation
explanation:
Both structures achieve O(log n) per operation, but a Fenwick tree's index arithmetic is simpler,
cache-friendlier, and requires roughly half the code and memory of a segment tree for this restricted use case.

title: Cousins in Binary Tree
question:
Two nodes are cousins if they are at the same depth but have different parents. What BFS metadata suffices to
check this?
options: C) Both depth and parent for each node
explanation:
Nodes are cousins iff depth(a)==depth(b) AND parent(a)!=parent(b). BFS naturally tracks depth
(level); you augment with parent references to distinguish cousins from siblings.

title: Compressed Trie Space Advantage
question: A compressed (Patricia) Trie for n keys with average key length L reduces node count from O(n*L) to what?
explanation:
A Patricia Trie merges chains of single-child nodes into single edges. The number of internal nodes is
at most n-1 and the number of leaves is n, giving O(n) nodes total regardless of key length.

title: BST Validation Using Range
question:
The correct approach to validate a BST uses:
return isValid(n->left, minVal, n->val) &&
options: A) Only comparing parent and child values
B) Passing min/max bounds down the recursion — shown above
C) In-order traversal and checking sorted order
D) Both B and C are equally correct
explanation:
Option C (in-order check) is also valid but Option B is the canonical recursive approach shown. Only
the range-propagation correctly enforces that all left-subtree values are less than the root, not just immediate
children.

title: 2D Segment Tree Use Case
question:
You need range sum queries on a 2D matrix where point updates occur frequently. Which structure is most
appropriate?
options: A) 1D Segment Tree with row merging
explanation:
A 2D Fenwick Tree supports O(log M * log N) point update and range sum query for an M×N matrix
with O(M*N) space — better constant factors than a 2D segment tree for this specific use case.

title: Boundary Traversal
question: Boundary traversal of a binary tree visits nodes in which order?
options: B) Left boundary (top-down), leaf nodes (left-right), right boundary (bottom-up)
explanation:
Boundary traversal: (1) left boundary excluding leaves top-to-bottom, (2) all leaf nodes left-to-right, (3)
right boundary excluding leaves bottom-to-top. This traces the outer perimeter of the tree.

title: Deletion Rotations
question: After deleting a node from an AVL tree, how many rotations may be required to restore balance?
options: C) O(log n) — rotations may propagate up the entire tree
explanation:
Unlike insertion which requires at most 2 rotations, AVL deletion may require rebalancing at every
ancestor up to the root, totalling O(log n) rotations.

title: Maximum Width of Binary Tree
question:
Maximum width (maximum number of nodes at any level) of a binary tree can be found using BFS in what
complexity?
options: B) O(n log n) time, O(1) space
explanation:
BFS processes all n nodes once (O(n) time). The queue holds at most the widest level, which can be
O(n/2) = O(n) nodes.

title: XOR Maximization with Trie
question:
To find the maximum XOR of two numbers in an array, a bit-level Trie is built and queried. What is the time
complexity?
explanation:
Building the Trie: O(32n) insertions, each O(32). Querying for each element: O(32n). Total: O(n) since
32 is the constant bit width of integers.

title: Offline vs Online Range Queries
question:
Merge Sort Tree supports online (arbitrary order) range queries in O(log^2 n). What does it sacrifice vs offline
approaches?
options: B) Time constant — offline approaches (e.g., persistent segment tree) can achieve O(log n) per query
D) It can only handle sorted input
explanation:
Offline methods like persistence allow O(log n) queries by reusing immutable structure versions.
Merge Sort Tree is online (answers queries as they arrive) but pays O(log^2 n).

title: Recover BST with Two Swapped Nodes
question: Two nodes in a BST are accidentally swapped. In-order traversal will reveal them as:
options: A) The first and last elements
B) Either one or two inversions (adjacent or non-adjacent swap)
C) The root and a leaf
D) Cannot be detected by in-order
explanation:
If swapped nodes are adjacent in in-order, there is one inversion (first > second). If non-adjacent,
there are two inversions. The first element of the first inversion and the second element of the last inversion are the
swapped nodes.

title: Black Height Guarantee
question: A Red-Black Tree with black-height k has at least how many internal nodes?
explanation:
In a tree with black-height k, if all nodes were black (minimum nodes), it would be a perfect binary tree
with height k and 2^k - 1 nodes.

title: Binary Tree to DLL Conversion
question: Converting a binary tree to a doubly linked list in-place using in-order traversal requires what extra space?
explanation:
The conversion is done during in-order traversal, which uses O(h) stack space for recursion. No
additional data structures are needed.

title: Palindrome Pairs Using Trie
question: For the 'Palindrome Pairs' problem with n words, using a Trie achieves what complexity vs brute force?
options: B) Trie: O(n * L^2), Brute Force: O(n^2 * L)
C) Trie: O(n * L), Brute Force: O(n^2)
D) Trie: O(n * L * log n), Brute Force: O(n^2 * L)
explanation:
With a Trie, for each word of length L, we check all O(L) prefixes and suffixes for palindrome
conditions in O(L) each, giving O(L^2) per word and O(n*L^2) total. Brute force checks all n^2 pairs, each in O(L).

title: Construct Tree from Inorder and Preorder
question:
Reconstructing a binary tree from inorder + preorder traversals. Using a hash map for inorder indices reduces
complexity from O(n^2) to?
explanation:
With a hash map, each preorder node lookup in the inorder array is O(1). Processing n nodes with
O(1) each gives O(n) total.

title: Merge Sort Tree Range Kth Smallest
question: A Merge Sort Tree can answer 'k-th smallest in range [l,r]' in what time?
options: C) O(log^3 n) with binary search + fractional cascading
explanation:
Binary search on the answer value, with each check requiring O(log^2 n) time in the Merge Sort Tree,
gives O(log^3 n). With fractional cascading, it reduces to O(log^2 n).

title: Threaded Binary Tree Advantage
question: A threaded binary tree's primary advantage is:
options: C) In-order traversal without stack or recursion (O(1) space)
explanation:
Threaded trees use otherwise-null right (and sometimes left) pointers to point to the in-order
successor (or predecessor). This enables stack-free, recursion-free in-order traversal in O(1) extra space.

title: Shortest Path in Unweighted Graph
question: Why does BFS guarantee shortest path in an unweighted, undirected graph?
options: B) BFS uses a priority queue
C) BFS expands nodes in non-decreasing order of edge count from source
explanation:
BFS explores all nodes at distance d before any node at distance d+1. The first time a node is
discovered, it is via the fewest edges, which equals the shortest path in unweighted graphs.

title: DFS Time Complexity on Sparse Graphs
question: For a directed graph with V vertices and E edges, DFS runs in:
explanation:
DFS visits each vertex once (O(V)) and traverses each edge once (O(E)), giving O(V+E). For sparse
graphs (E << V^2), this is much better than O(V^2) matrix-based approaches.

title: Dijkstra with Negative Edges
question: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative edge weights?
options: A) It cannot handle directed graphs
B) Once a node is marked visited with tentative distance d, a later negative edge could yield a shorter path, which Dijkstra ignores
C) The priority queue becomes corrupted
D) It always gives the wrong answer on negative graphs
explanation:
Dijkstra's greedy choice assumes that the minimum tentative distance is final. Negative edges
invalidate this: a longer path with a negative edge can beat a shorter path with positive edges after the node is
'settled'.

title: Kahn's Algorithm — BFS Topological Sort
question: Kahn's algorithm for topological sort uses:
options: B) In-degree array + queue processing zero-in-degree nodes
C) Priority queue on node weights
explanation:
Kahn's: initialize a queue with all nodes of in-degree 0. Repeatedly dequeue a node, add it to the
result, and decrement in-degrees of its neighbors; enqueue any that reach 0. If result size < V, a cycle exists.

title: Detecting Cycle with Topological Sort
question: In Kahn's algorithm, if the topological sort produces fewer than V vertices, what does it indicate?
explanation:
Nodes in a cycle never reach in-degree 0 (each is always waiting for another in-cycle node to be
removed). Fewer than V nodes in the output means at least one cycle exists.

title: Dijkstra Priority Queue Implementation
question: Using a binary heap (priority_queue), Dijkstra's algorithm on V vertices and E edges runs in:
explanation:
Each vertex is extracted from the heap once: O(V log V). Each edge may trigger a relaxation/heap
push: O(E log V). Total: O((V+E) log V). With a Fibonacci heap, this reduces to O(E + V log V).

title: Union by Rank + Path Compression Amortized Cost
question: With both union by rank and path compression, the amortized cost per DSU operation is:
options: C) O( α (n)) — inverse Ackermann, effectively O(1)
explanation:
The inverse Ackermann function α (n) grows so slowly that α (n) ≤ 4 for all practical n (n < 10^80000).
Combined union-by-rank and path compression achieves this near-constant amortized complexity.

title: Kruskal's MST with DSU
question:
Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree algorithm sorts edges and uses DSU. Its total time complexity is dominated
by:
options: A) O(E log E) for sorting edges
C) O(E * α (V)) for union-find operations
explanation:
Sorting E edges takes O(E log E). The union-find operations for all edges take O(E * α (V)) ≈ O(E).
Sorting dominates, giving O(E log E) overall.

title: Multi-source BFS for 0-1 Matrix
question: In the '01 Matrix' problem (distance to nearest 0 for each cell), multi-source BFS initializes the queue with:
options: B) All cells with value 0 simultaneously
explanation:
Multi-source BFS starts all '0' cells at distance 0 simultaneously. BFS then naturally propagates
minimum distances to '1' cells, correctly computing the nearest-0 distance for every cell in O(m*n).

title: Tarjan's Bridge-Finding — Key Property
question: In Tarjan's bridge-finding algorithm, an edge (u,v) is a bridge if:
explanation:
low[v] > disc[u] means no back-edge from the subtree rooted at v can reach u or its ancestors, so
removing edge (u,v) disconnects the graph — it's a bridge.

title: Tarjan's SCC Algorithm Time Complexity
question: Tarjan's Strongly Connected Components algorithm runs in:
explanation:
Tarjan's SCC does a single DFS pass maintaining a stack and low-link values. Each vertex and edge
is processed once: O(V+E).

title: Bellman-Ford vs Dijkstra Trade-off
question: Bellman-Ford is preferred over Dijkstra when:
options: A) The graph has no negative cycles
B) The graph has negative edge weights (and you want to detect negative cycles)
explanation:
Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles by running V-1 relaxation
passes. Its O(VE) complexity is worse than Dijkstra's O((V+E) log V), but it's correct for negative-weight graphs.

title: Floyd-Warshall Space Complexity
question: Floyd-Warshall all-pairs shortest path uses how much space?
explanation:
Floyd-Warshall maintains a V×V distance matrix (and optionally a predecessor matrix), requiring
O(V^2) space. The algorithm itself runs in O(V^3) time.

title: Bipartite Graph Detection
question: BFS-based bipartite graph detection assigns two colors to nodes. The graph is bipartite if and only if:
options: A) All nodes of the same color are connected
B) No edge connects two nodes of the same color
D) There are exactly two connected components
explanation:
A graph is bipartite if vertices can be 2-colored such that no edge connects same-colored vertices.
BFS colors each neighbor opposite to the current node; if a conflict is found, the graph is not bipartite.

title: Detecting Cycle in Undirected Graph with DSU
question: Using DSU to detect a cycle in an undirected graph: a cycle exists when?
options: A) Two vertices have the same rank
B) An edge (u,v) is found where find(u) == find(v)
C) The union operation returns false
D) Any component has more edges than vertices
explanation:
If find(u) == find(v) before union, nodes u and v are already in the same component. Adding edge
(u,v) would create a cycle.

title: Network Flow — Ford-Fulkerson Termination
question: Ford-Fulkerson may not terminate if edge capacities are:
explanation:
With irrational capacities, augmenting paths may yield augmenting flows that sum to a series that
doesn't converge to the max flow. Edmonds-Karp (BFS-based) guarantees termination regardless.

title: Prim's vs Kruskal's — Dense vs Sparse
question: For a dense graph (E ≈ V^2), which MST algorithm is preferred?
options: A) Prim's with adjacency matrix — O(V^2)
B) Kruskal's — O(E log E) = O(V^2 log V)
explanation:
For dense graphs, Prim's with an adjacency matrix runs in O(V^2), better than Kruskal's O(E log E) =
O(V^2 log V). For sparse graphs, Kruskal's with DSU is preferred.

title: Topological Sort via DFS
question: In DFS-based topological sort, vertices are added to the result in:
options: B) Post-order reversed (when DFS finishes a vertex)
explanation:
A vertex is pushed onto a stack when its DFS finishes (all descendants are processed). Reversing
this post-order gives a valid topological ordering.

title: Shortest Path in DAG
question: For a DAG, the most efficient shortest path algorithm is:
options: C) Topological sort + single relaxation pass in O(V+E)
explanation:
In a DAG, topological ordering ensures each vertex is relaxed after all predecessors. One pass in
topological order relaxes all edges correctly, with O(V+E) complexity and no need for negative-edge handling.

title: Articulation Points vs Bridges
question: What is the condition for a vertex u to be an articulation point in Tarjan's algorithm?
options: A) low[v] > disc[u] for all children v
B) u is root with 2+ children, OR u is non-root and has a child v with low[v] >= disc[u]
C) u has the highest disc value
D) u is connected to every other vertex
explanation:
For non-root u: child v with low[v] >= disc[u] means no back-edge from v's subtree goes above u, so
removing u disconnects v. For root: it's an articulation point iff it has 2+ children in the DFS tree.

title: Offline LCA with DSU (Tarjan's LCA)
question: Tarjan's offline LCA algorithm processes queries in what order?
options: B) DFS post-order with union-find to track ancestors
explanation:
Tarjan's offline LCA does DFS. When a node u finishes, it's unioned with its parent. When processing
a query (u,v): if v is already visited, LCA(u,v) = find(v). All queries must be known upfront (offline).

title: A* vs Dijkstra
question: A* outperforms Dijkstra by:
options: B) Using a heuristic to prioritize exploration toward the goal, reducing nodes examined
C) Running in O(V) instead of O(V log V)
explanation:
A* uses f(n) = g(n) + h(n) where h is an admissible heuristic estimating cost to goal. This focuses the
search, potentially examining far fewer nodes than Dijkstra's uniform expansion.

title: Word Ladder — BFS Level Count
question:
In the Word Ladder problem, BFS gives the minimum transformation sequence. If no sequence exists, BFS
returns:
explanation:
By convention (LeetCode definition), if no transformation sequence exists, return 0. BFS naturally
handles this: if the target is never reached, return 0 after exhausting all possibilities.

title: Euler Circuit Condition
question: A connected undirected graph has an Euler circuit (visits every edge exactly once, returns to start) iff:
options: B) Every vertex has even degree
explanation:
Euler's theorem: an Euler circuit exists iff the graph is connected and every vertex has even degree. If
exactly 2 vertices have odd degree, an Euler path (not circuit) exists between them.

title: Hamiltonian Path NP-Completeness
question: Unlike Euler paths, Hamiltonian paths (visit every vertex exactly once) are:
options: A) Solvable in O(V + E) with DFS
B) NP-complete — no known polynomial algorithm
explanation:
The Hamiltonian path problem is NP-complete. No polynomial algorithm is known. The best exact
algorithms are exponential (O(2^n * n) with bitmask DP). Contrast with Euler paths which are O(E).

title: DFS Edge Classification
question: In DFS on a directed graph, a 'cross edge' is:
options: A) An edge to an ancestor in the DFS tree
B) An edge within the same DFS tree
C) An edge from one DFS subtree to another (or a different DFS tree component)
D) An edge that creates a cycle
explanation:
DFS classifies edges as: tree edges (in DFS tree), back edges (to ancestor, indicating cycle), forward
edges (to descendant, directed only), cross edges (between unrelated subtrees or components, directed only).

title: Max Flow Min Cut Theorem
question: The Max-Flow Min-Cut theorem states:
options: A) Maximum flow equals the sum of all edge capacities
B) Maximum flow in a network equals the minimum capacity cut separating source from sink
C) Min cut is always unique
D) Max flow can be computed in O(V) time
explanation:
Max-Flow Min-Cut is a fundamental theorem: the maximum amount of flow from source to sink equals
the minimum total capacity of edges that, if removed, would disconnect source from sink.

title: Rotting Oranges — Multi-source BFS
question: In the 'Rotting Oranges' problem, the answer (minimum minutes) equals:
options: B) BFS levels from all initially rotten oranges minus 1 (or -1 if unreachable)
D) Number of initially rotten oranges
explanation:
Multi-source BFS from all initially rotten oranges spreads in BFS levels. The number of levels
traversed (minutes elapsed) until no fresh oranges remain is the answer.

title: Path Compression Variants
question:
Which path compression technique achieves the best amortized complexity while being simpler to implement
than full compression?
options: C) Both path splitting and path halving achieve the same O( α (n)) complexity
explanation:
Both path splitting (make every node point to its grandparent on the find path) and path halving (same
but every other node) achieve the same O( α (n)) amortized complexity as full path compression, with simpler
implementation.

title: Johnson's Algorithm Use Case
question: Johnson's algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths is efficient when:
options: B) Graph is sparse — it runs in O(V^2 log V + VE), beating Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) for sparse graphs
C) All edge weights are positive
explanation:
Johnson's reweights edges using Bellman-Ford to eliminate negatives, then runs Dijkstra from each
vertex. For sparse E = O(V), this is O(V^2 log V), far better than Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3).

title: SCC in Social Network Analysis
question: In a directed social graph (follow relationships), a Strongly Connected Component represents:
options: A) Users with the most followers
B) Users connected by exactly two edges
C) A group where every user can reach every other user by following links
explanation:
An SCC is a maximal subgraph where every vertex is reachable from every other. In social networks,
this represents closed communities where all members can communicate through directed follow chains.

title: Biconnected Components vs SCCs
question: Biconnected components apply to which type of graph?
options: A) Undirected graphs — maximal subgraphs with no articulation points
explanation:
Biconnected components partition the edges of undirected graphs into maximal subgraphs that
remain connected when any single vertex is removed. SCCs apply to directed graphs.

title: BFS on Implicit Graph — Sliding Puzzle
question: For the 8-puzzle (3x3 sliding tiles), BFS finds the minimum moves. The state space size is:
explanation:
The 9 tiles can be arranged in 9! ways, but exactly half are reachable from any given state (parity
invariant), giving 9!/2 = 181,440 reachable states. BFS is feasible.

title: DFS on Grid — Number of Islands
question: DFS-based 'Number of Islands' solution: what terminates the recursion for each island?
options: B) Hitting boundary or water cells ('0') or already-visited cells
explanation:
DFS from a '1' cell recursively marks connected land cells as visited (e.g., '0' or '#'). Recursion stops
at boundaries, water cells, or already-visited cells. Each DFS call from an unvisited '1' finds one island.

title: Strongly Connected Component — Kosaraju's Two-Pass
question: Kosaraju's SCC algorithm performs:
options: A) BFS twice on the original graph
B) DFS on original graph (recording finish order), then DFS on reversed graph in reverse finish order
C) DFS once with back-edge tracking
explanation:
Pass 1: DFS on G, push vertices to stack in finish order. Pass 2: reverse G, pop vertices and DFS;
each DFS tree in pass 2 is an SCC. Two full DFS passes, O(V+E) total.

title: Minimum Spanning Tree Uniqueness
question: An MST is unique when:
options: B) All edge weights are integers
C) All edge weights are distinct
explanation:
If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is unique. The proof uses the cycle property: the unique
maximum-weight edge in any cycle is never in the MST. With ties, multiple MSTs of the same weight may exist.

title: 0-1 BFS with Deque
question:
0-1 BFS solves shortest path where edges have weight 0 or 1 using a deque. Why is it O(V+E) instead of
O((V+E) log V)?
options: A) Uses a Fibonacci heap internally
B) Weight-0 edges push to front of deque, weight-1 to back, maintaining sorted order without heap overhead
explanation:
By pushing weight-0 edges to the front and weight-1 to the back, the deque always has the
minimum-distance node at the front — like a heap but O(1) per push, giving O(V+E) total.

title: Traveling Salesman — DP Bitmask
question: The bitmask DP solution for TSP on n cities has complexity:
explanation:
State: dp[mask][i] = min cost to visit cities in 'mask', ending at city i. There are O(2^n * n) states, each
requiring O(n) transitions. Total: O(2^n * n^2). Still exponential but much better than O(n!).

title: DSU with Rollback for Offline Queries
question:
DSU with rollback (union by rank without path compression) supports undo in O(log n). Why can't path
compression be used with rollback?
options: B) Path compression uses more memory
C) Path compression irreversibly modifies parent pointers, making undo impossible without storing entire path history
D) Path compression conflicts with rank
explanation:
Path compression restructures the tree, flattening it. To undo a union, you need to restore the original
parent pointers. With path compression, intermediate pointers were changed and aren't easy to restore. Union by
rank only changes two pointers per union, trivially undoable.

title: Network Flow — Dinic's Algorithm Complexity
question: Dinic's algorithm for max flow has complexity:
explanation:
Dinic's builds blocking flows in a level graph using BFS + DFS. There are O(V) phases (BFS levels
increase by at least 1 each phase), each blocking flow takes O(VE). Total: O(V^2 * E), or O(E * sqrt(V)) for unit
capacity networks.

title: Shortest Cycle Detection
question: Finding the shortest cycle (girth) in an unweighted undirected graph runs in:
options: B) O(V * (V + E)) — BFS from each vertex
explanation:
Run BFS from each vertex; when BFS finds an edge to an already-visited same-level node, a cycle is
detected. The shortest such cycle across all BFS runs is the girth. V BFS runs of O(V+E) each: O(V*(V+E)).

title: Boggle Solver — DFS + Trie
question: A Boggle solver DFS on an N×N board with a Trie of W words. What is the time complexity?
options: C) O(N^2 * 4^L) where L is max word length, pruned by Trie
explanation:
DFS from each of N^2 cells explores at most 4^L paths of length L. The Trie prunes branches with no
matching prefix early. In practice, much faster, but the theoretical bound is O(N^2 * 4^L).

title: Minimum Cost Maximum Flow Application
question: Min-Cost Max-Flow is used to solve which type of problem?
options: C) Assignment problems and transportation optimization (e.g., minimizing cost while satisfying supply-demand constraints)
explanation:
Min-Cost Max-Flow finds the maximum flow from source to sink while minimizing total cost. It solves
assignment problems, job scheduling, and transportation problems where both flow and cost must be optimized.

title: Alien Dictionary — Topological Sort
question: Given a sorted list of alien words, the character ordering is derived by:
options: A) Comparing all pairs of characters
B) Finding the first differing character between adjacent words to build edges, then topological sort
explanation:
Compare each adjacent pair of words; the first character difference gives a directed edge (c1 → c2
meaning c1 comes before c2 in the alien alphabet). Topological sort on these edges gives the ordering.

title: Critical Connections in Network — Bridge Finding
question: LeetCode 'Critical Connections in Network': which algorithm directly solves this?
explanation:
Critical connections are edges whose removal increases the number of connected components —
exactly the definition of bridges. Tarjan's algorithm finds all bridges in O(V+E).

title: Bipartite Matching — Hopcroft-Karp Complexity
question: Hopcroft-Karp algorithm for maximum bipartite matching runs in:
explanation:
Hopcroft-Karp finds maximal augmenting paths in phases using BFS + DFS. There are O(sqrt(V))
phases, each requiring O(E) work. Total: O(E * sqrt(V)), significantly better than the O(VE) naive approach.

title: Weighted DSU for Relative Ranking
question: Weighted DSU (Union-Find with edge weights) can solve which type of problem?
options: B) Problems involving relative ordering or distance between elements (e.g., 'how many times heavier is A than B?')
explanation:
Weighted DSU maintains a weight relative to the root for each node. It can answer questions like
'what is the ratio between elements X and Y?' — used in problems like 'Evaluate Division' on LeetCode.

title: PageRank — Graph Centrality
question: PageRank is computed iteratively as a form of:
options: B) Topological sort of web pages
C) Power iteration on the graph's adjacency matrix (dominant eigenvector computation)
D) Dijkstra's on page link weights
explanation:
PageRank iteratively applies the transition matrix (normalized adjacency) until convergence,
computing the stationary distribution of a random walk — equivalent to finding the dominant eigenvector of the
transition matrix.

title: Jump Game II — BFS Greedy Levels
question: Jump Game II (minimum jumps to reach end) can be modeled as BFS where each 'level' represents:
options: A) Each index in the array
C) All indices reachable with exactly k jumps (implicit BFS levels)
explanation:
Track the farthest index reachable within each 'level' (same number of jumps). When the current
position crosses the previous level's boundary, increment jumps. This greedy BFS-level approach runs in O(n).

title: Course Schedule II — Prerequisites as DAG
question: 'Course Schedule II' maps to finding a topological sort of a directed graph. If the graph has a cycle:
options: B) Return empty array — no valid course ordering exists
explanation:
If prerequisites form a cycle (A requires B, B requires C, C requires A), no valid ordering exists.
Kahn's algorithm detects this when the topological sort output has fewer vertices than the total number of courses.

title: 0/1 Knapsack State Definition
question: In 0/1 Knapsack with n items and capacity W, the DP state dp[i][w] represents:
options: A) Number of items selected up to index i
B) Remaining capacity after i items
C) Maximum value achievable using items 0..i with weight limit w
D) Minimum weight for value i
explanation:
dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with weight capacity w. Recurrence: dp[i][w] = max(dp[i-1][w],
dp[i-1][w-weight[i]] + value[i]) if weight[i] <= w, else dp[i-1][w].

title: Knapsack Space Optimization
question: 0/1 Knapsack can be solved in O(W) space (instead of O(n*W)) by:
options: A) Iterating capacity from W down to weight[i] prevents using item i twice
C) Using two arrays and swapping
explanation:
Backward iteration ensures that when we compute dp[w], dp[w-weight[i]] still reflects the state
BEFORE item i was considered (previous row), maintaining the 0/1 constraint. Forward iteration would allow
picking item i multiple times (unbounded knapsack).

title: Unbounded Knapsack vs 0/1
question: The key difference between 0/1 and Unbounded Knapsack recurrences:
options: B) Unbounded: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w-weight[i]] + value[i]) with FORWARD iteration; 0/1 uses backward
explanation:
In unbounded knapsack, each item can be used unlimited times. Forward iteration allows item i to be
selected again in the same pass (dp[w-weight[i]] already reflects item i being chosen). 0/1 uses backward to
prevent this.

title: LCS Length — Output Prediction
question: Compute LCS length for s1 = 'ABCBDAB' and s2 = 'BDCAB'.
explanation:
The LCS is 'BCAB' or 'BDAB' of length 4. The DP table confirms this via the standard O(m*n)
recurrence.

title: LCS to LIS Reduction
question: Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS) can be reduced to LCS by computing LCS of the array with:
explanation:
LIS(A) = LCS(A, sorted_unique(A)). An element appears in the LIS iff it appears in both A (in order)
and the sorted unique version. This runs in O(n^2) via LCS; patience sorting gives O(n log n) directly.

title: Edit Distance — Three Operations
question: The edit distance (Levenshtein) DP recurrence dp[i][j] = ?
options: B) If s[i]==t[j]: dp[i-1][j-1]; else 1+min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1])
explanation:
If characters match, no operation needed: take dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise, take minimum of: delete from s
(dp[i-1][j]+1), insert into s (dp[i][j-1]+1), or replace (dp[i-1][j-1]+1).

title: Matrix Chain Multiplication — State
question: In Matrix Chain Multiplication DP, dp[i][j] represents:
options: A) Cost to multiply matrix i and j
B) Minimum scalar multiplications to compute the product of matrices i through j
D) Number of ways to parenthesize matrices i..j
explanation:
dp[i][j] = min cost to multiply the chain of matrices from index i to j. Recurrence: dp[i][j] = min over k of
(dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + dims[i-1]*dims[k]*dims[j]).

title: MCM Time Complexity
question: Matrix Chain Multiplication DP has time complexity:
explanation:
There are O(n^2) subproblems (all pairs i,j), and each requires O(n) work to try all split points k. Total:
O(n^3). Space is O(n^2).

title: Tower of Hanoi — Minimum Moves
question: The minimum number of moves to solve Tower of Hanoi with n disks is:
explanation:
T(n) = 2*T(n-1) + 1 (move top n-1 to auxiliary, move nth disk, move n-1 back). Solving: T(n) = 2^n - 1.
For 64 disks: 2^64 - 1 ≈ 1.8 × 10^19 moves.

title: Coin Change — Fewest Coins
question:
For coin denominations [1,5,6,9] and amount 11, the greedy approach (pick largest) gives 3 coins (9+1+1). DP
gives:
explanation:
Greedy fails here. DP correctly identifies 5+6=11 using 2 coins, proving that coin change requires DP
(or BFS), not greedy, for arbitrary denominations.

title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
question: LPS(s) is related to LCS by:
explanation:
A palindromic subsequence reads the same forwards and backwards, so it's a common subsequence
of s and its reverse. LPS(s) = LCS(s, reverse(s)).

title: Wildcard Matching — DP Bug
options: A) No bug — this is correct. dp[i-1][j] handles '*' matching one+ chars, dp[i][j-1] handles '*' matching empty
C) '?' should match any number of chars
explanation:
The code is correct. '*' can match any sequence: dp[i-1][j] means '*' matches one more character from
s; dp[i][j-1] means '*' matches empty string. The initialization correctly handles patterns starting with '*'.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
question: 'Partition Equal Subset Sum' reduces to which well-known DP problem?
explanation:
If total sum is odd, return false. Otherwise, check if a subset sums to total/2 using 0/1 Knapsack DP.
dp[w] = true if some subset sums to exactly w.

title: Memoization vs Tabulation Trade-offs
question: When is top-down memoization preferred over bottom-up tabulation?
options: B) When only a fraction of subproblems need to be computed (sparse dependency graph)
C) When space is the primary constraint
explanation:
If the recursion only visits a small fraction of all possible states (e.g., a sparse dependency graph),
memoization avoids computing unnecessary states. Tabulation always fills all states, even irrelevant ones.

title: Rod Cutting — Unbounded Knapsack Variant
question: Rod cutting (maximize revenue from cutting a rod of length n with given piece prices) is a variant of:
options: B) Unbounded Knapsack — each piece length can be used multiple times
explanation:
Each cut length can be reused any number of times (a piece of length 2 can be cut multiple times
from a rod of length 8). This maps directly to Unbounded Knapsack.

title: Burst Balloons — Interval DP
question: 'Burst Balloons' uses interval DP where dp[i][j] means:
options: A) Number of ways to burst balloons i to j
B) Maximum coins from bursting all balloons between i and j (exclusive boundaries)
C) Minimum coins to burst balloons i to j
D) Sum of balloon values from i to j
explanation:
dp[i][j] = max coins obtainable by bursting all balloons strictly between indices i and j (i and j are
boundaries not burst in this range). The key insight: think of k as the LAST balloon burst in range (i,j), not the first.

title: Longest Common Substring vs Subsequence
question: The key difference between LCS (Longest Common Subsequence) and Longest Common Substring (LCStr):
options: A) LCS is O(n^2), LCStr is O(n^3)
B) LCS allows gaps (subsequence); LCStr requires contiguity. LCStr resets dp[i][j] to 0 when characters don't match
C) LCStr is always longer than LCS
explanation:
LCS: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1 if match, else max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). LCStr: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1 if
match, else 0. LCStr tracks the max seen; no gap allowed.

title: DP on Trees — Maximum Independent Set
question:
Maximum Independent Set on a tree: dp[v][0] = max nodes in subtree of v when v is NOT selected, dp[v][1] =
max when v IS selected. Recurrence for dp[v][1]?
options: A) 1 + sum of dp[c][1] for children c
B) 1 + sum of dp[c][0] for children c — if v is selected, no child can be selected
C) sum of max(dp[c][0], dp[c][1]) for children c
explanation:
If vertex v is included, none of its children can be included (independent set constraint). So dp[v][1] =
1 + sum(dp[c][0]) over all children c. dp[v][0] = sum(max(dp[c][0], dp[c][1])) since children can independently be in
or out.

title: Palindrome Partitioning — DP State
question: 'Palindrome Partitioning II' (minimum cuts for palindromic partition): dp[i] represents:
options: A) Number of palindromes ending at i
B) Minimum cuts needed for s[0..i]
C) Length of longest palindrome ending at i
D) Number of ways to partition s[0..i]
explanation:
dp[i] = min cuts for s[0..i]. Transition: dp[i] = min(dp[j-1] + 1) for all j<=i where s[j..i] is a palindrome.
Pre-compute palindrome table using DP or Manacher's O(n) algorithm for optimization.

title: Subset Sum — Exponential Baseline
question: Naive recursive subset sum explores how many subsets for n elements?
explanation:
Each of n elements can be included or excluded: 2^n subsets. Naive recursion without memoization
explores all 2^n possibilities. DP reduces this to O(n*W) pseudo-polynomial time.

title: Number of Distinct Subsequences
question: dp[i][j] in 'Distinct Subsequences' (count ways s's subsequences equal t) represents:
options: A) Length of LCS up to s[i] and t[j]
B) Number of ways s[0..i-1] contains t[0..j-1] as a subsequence
C) Edit distance between s[0..i] and t[0..j]
explanation:
dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] (don't use s[i]) + dp[i-1][j-1] if s[i-1]==t[j-1] (use s[i] to match t[j]). Base: dp[i][0]=1
(empty t matched always), dp[0][j]=0 for j>0.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram — Stack DP
question: The 'Largest Rectangle in Histogram' optimal solution uses:
options: B) Segment tree for range minimum
C) Monotonic stack in O(n) time
D) Divide and conquer in O(n log n)
explanation:
A monotonic increasing stack tracks bars. When a shorter bar is encountered, pop bars and compute
rectangle area (popped height * width since last shorter bar). O(n) total since each bar is pushed/popped once.

title: Catalan Numbers — DP
code: Catalan number C_n counts many things. C_n = sum of C_i * C_{n-1-i} for i=0 to n-1. This recurrence relates to:
options: A) Number of spanning trees of K_n
B) Number of valid BSTs with n keys, number of valid parenthesizations, Dyck paths
C) Number of prime numbers up to n
D) Number of permutations of n elements
explanation:
Catalan numbers count: valid BSTs with n distinct keys, ways to parenthesize n+1 matrices (MCM),
Dyck paths of length 2n, valid bracket sequences of length 2n, triangulations of polygon with n+2 sides, and many
more.

title: Generate Permutations — Backtracking Complexity
question: Generating all permutations of n distinct elements via backtracking has time complexity:
explanation:
There are n! permutations, each of length n to write/copy. Total work: O(n * n!). The recursion tree has
n! leaves, but internal nodes sum to another factor.

title: Stock Buy Sell with Cooldown
question: 'Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown': after selling, you must wait 1 day. The DP states needed are:
options: A) dp[i] = max profit on day i
B) held[i], sold[i], rest[i] — three states per day
D) dp[i][j] where j is number of transactions
explanation:
Three states capture all transitions: held[i] = max profit holding stock on day i; sold[i] = max profit just
sold on day i; rest[i] = max profit in cooldown/rest on day i. Transitions encode the cooldown rule naturally.

title: Interleaving String — 2D DP
question: 'Interleaving String' (can s3 be formed by interleaving s1 and s2) uses dp[i][j] where:
options: A) dp[i][j] = LCS of s1[0..i] and s2[0..j]
B) dp[i][j] = true if s3[0..i+j-1] can be formed by interleaving s1[0..i-1] and s2[0..j-1]
C) dp[i][j] = edit distance between s1[0..i] and s3[0..j]
explanation:
dp[i][j] = (dp[i-1][j] && s1[i-1]==s3[i+j-1]) || (dp[i][j-1] && s2[j-1]==s3[i+j-1]). Base case dp[0][0]=true.
Answer is dp[m][n].

title: Palindrome Substrings — Count
question: 'Count Palindromic Substrings': the expand-around-center technique runs in:
options: C) O(n) with Manacher's (but Manacher's finds longest, not count directly)
explanation:
For each of the 2n-1 centers (n odd-length, n-1 even-length), expand while palindrome. Total
expansions across all centers: O(n^2). Manacher's achieves O(n) for the longest palindrome but counting all
requires O(n^2) without extensions.

title: Jump Game II — DP vs Greedy
question: Jump Game II solved with DP has O(n^2) complexity. The greedy approach achieves:
explanation:
Greedy: track current range end and farthest reachable. When index reaches range end, increment
jumps and extend range to farthest. Single O(n) pass suffices, avoiding the O(n^2) DP.

title: N-Queens — Backtracking State
question: N-Queens backtracking maintains which sets for O(1) conflict checking?
options: B) Sets for: columns, left diagonals (row-col), and right diagonals (row+col)
C) Sets for rows and columns
explanation:
Three hash sets: columns used, left diagonals (constant row-col), right diagonals (constant row+col).
Checking if a position (r,c) is safe is O(1) with these sets vs O(n) scanning the board.

title: Longest Increasing Path in Matrix
question: 'Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix' uses memoized DFS. The time complexity is:
options: B) O(m*n) — each cell computed once via memoization
explanation:
Each cell is the starting point of at most one DFS computation (subsequent calls hit the memo cache).
Each cell has at most 4 neighbors. Total work: O(4*m*n) = O(m*n).

title: Decode Ways — State Machine DP
question: 'Decode Ways' (count ways to decode a digit string as letters): dp[i] depends on:
options: C) dp[i-1] if s[i] is valid single digit, + dp[i-2] if s[i-1..i] is valid two-digit (10-26)
explanation:
At each position i, you can decode one digit (if valid, adds dp[i-1] ways) or two digits (if 10-26, adds
dp[i-2] ways). Handle '0' carefully: '0' alone is invalid; only '10' and '20' are valid two-digit.

title: Word Break — DP + Trie
question: 'Word Break' (can string s be segmented into dictionary words) with a Trie for the dictionary runs in:
options: B) O(n^2) with hash set, or O(n * L) with Trie where L is max word length
C) O(n * W) where W is total characters in dictionary
explanation:
dp[i] = true if s[0..i-1] is segmentable. For each i, check all j < i: dp[j] && s[j..i-1] in dictionary. With
hash set: O(n^2) average. With Trie: at most L characters per position, so O(n*L).

title: Distinct BSTs — Catalan Number
question: The number of structurally unique BSTs with n keys is the n-th Catalan number. For n=4:
explanation:
Catalan numbers: C(0)=1, C(1)=1, C(2)=2, C(3)=5, C(4)=14. For each root k (1 to n), left subtree has
k-1 keys, right has n-k. C(n) = sum(C(k)*C(n-1-k)).

title: Memoization Space Overhead in Deep Recursion
question: A top-down DP with n states, each requiring O(k) space for its result, uses total space of:
options: B) O(n*k) for results + O(depth) for call stack
explanation:
The memo table stores n results, each of size k: O(n*k). The recursion call stack uses O(depth) =
O(n) in the worst case (linear chain). Total space: O(n*k + n) = O(n*k).

title: Maximum Subarray — Kadane's Insight
question: Kadane's algorithm DP insight: dp[i] = max subarray sum ending at index i =
explanation:
Either extend the previous subarray (dp[i-1] + a[i]) or start fresh at current element (a[i]). We choose
whichever is larger. This compresses a 2D DP to 1D, running in O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Minimum Path Sum in Grid
question: Grid DP for minimum path sum: dp[i][j] = ?
options: B) grid[i][j] + min(dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j]), with boundary handling for first row/col
explanation:
General recurrence: dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]). First row: only from left. First column:
only from above. Answer: dp[m-1][n-1].

title: Dice Roll Target Sum — Count Ways
question: Counting ways to get sum S with d dice, each having f faces. The DP table has dimensions:
explanation:
dp[i][j] = number of ways to get sum j using i dice. i ranges from 1 to d; j ranges from i to i*f. Table
size: O(d*S). Transition: dp[i][j] = sum(dp[i-1][j-k] for k=1 to f).

title: Combination Sum — Backtracking Termination
question:
In Combination Sum backtracking (elements can be reused, find all combinations summing to target), what
prevents infinite loops?
options: C) Remaining target decreases each recursive call; terminate when target == 0 or < 0
explanation:
Since all candidates are positive, subtracting any candidate strictly decreases the remaining target.
Recursion terminates when target hits 0 (found combination) or goes negative (dead end). No risk of infinite
recursion.

title: Regular Expression Matching — DP
question: In regex matching DP with '.' (any char) and '*' (zero or more), dp[i][j] when p[j-1]=='*' equals:
options: C) dp[i][j-2] (zero occurrences) OR (dp[i-1][j] if s[i-1] matches p[j-2])
explanation:
'*' can mean zero occurrences: dp[i][j-2]. Or one-or-more: dp[i-1][j] if the preceding character p[j-2]
matches s[i-1] (or p[j-2]=='.'). This is the critical case that handles multiple character repetitions.

title: Egg Drop — Optimal DP
question:
The classic Egg Drop problem with k eggs and n floors: the naive O(kn^2) DP can be optimized to O(kn log n)
using:
options: B) Binary search on the optimal floor to drop from (monotonic optimal structure)
explanation:
The 'check floor' function in the DP transition is monotonic: as the answer increases, the optimal drop
floor only increases. Binary search exploits this property to find the optimal floor in O(log n) instead of O(n),
improving total complexity.

title: Maximum Profit with K Transactions
question: 'Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV' (at most k transactions) DP complexity:
options: B) O(n * k) time with O(k) space optimization
explanation:
dp[i][j] = max profit with at most j transactions up to day i. With space optimization (rolling array on
transactions), O(n*k) time and O(k) space. If k >= n/2, unlimited transactions (greedy) gives O(n).

title: Subset Generation — Bitmask vs Backtracking
question: For generating all subsets of n elements, bitmask iteration vs backtracking have what time/space complexity?
options: A) Both O(2^n) time; bitmask O(1) extra space, backtracking O(n) stack space
D) Both O(n*2^n) time and O(n) space
explanation:
Both explore all 2^n subsets. Bitmask uses a loop variable (O(1) space). Backtracking uses the
recursion stack (O(n) depth). To print each subset of size up to n, each subset takes O(n), giving O(n*2^n) output
time for both.

title: Minimum Window Subsequence
question:
'Minimum Window Subsequence' (find shortest substring of S containing T as subsequence) optimal approach
is:
options: C) DP with backward scan: after finding T in S forward, scan backward to tighten window — O(n*m) but optimal in practice
explanation:
Forward scan finds an end position where T is a subsequence. Backward scan from that end finds the
tightest start. DP precomputes next occurrence of each character for O(n) scanning. Total O(n*m) or O(n *
|alphabet|) with preprocessing.

title: Maximal Square of 1s in Matrix
question: dp[i][j] in 'Maximal Square' (largest square of 1s) represents:
options: A) Number of 1s in row i up to column j
B) Side length of the largest square with (i,j) as its bottom-right corner
D) Number of squares ending at (i,j)
explanation:
dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1 if matrix[i][j]=='1', else 0. The minimum of the three
neighboring DP values limits the largest square that can extend to (i,j). Answer: max(dp[i][j])^2.

title: Flood Fill — DFS vs BFS
question:
Flood Fill (replace connected region of same color) can use DFS or BFS. For a worst-case m×n grid, stack
overflow risk exists with DFS when:
options: C) m*n is very large (millions of cells), causing recursion stack depth to exceed system limits
explanation:
In worst case, DFS recurses through all m*n connected cells, creating a call stack of depth O(m*n).
For large grids, this exceeds typical stack limits (~10^4-10^5 frames). BFS uses an explicit queue (heap-allocated)
and avoids this.

title: Longest Common Subsequence — Space Optimization
question: LCS(s1, s2) of length m and n uses O(m*n) space. The space-optimized version uses:
options: A) O(n) using a single array
B) O(n) using two rows (current and previous) or one array with careful traversal
explanation:
Since dp[i][j] only depends on dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], and dp[i-1][j-1], we can use two 1D arrays (prev and
curr) of size n+1, reducing space from O(m*n) to O(n). With a single array and a temp variable, O(n) space.

title: Dice Game — Expected Value DP
question:
In a dice game where you roll a fair 6-sided die and can stop at any time to collect the rolled value (or reroll),
what is the expected value of an optimal strategy?
options: B) Higher than 3.5 — reroll when value ≤ expected threshold, approximately 4.0
explanation:
Let E be the expected value. You keep the roll if it's > E, otherwise reroll. E = (1/6)*sum of values > E
+ (P(roll <= E))*E. Solving: E = 14/4 = 3.5? With optimal play: keep if die shows 4,5,6; E = (4+5+6)/3 * (3/6) +
E*(3/6) => E/2 = 5 => E ≈ 4.0.

title: Minimum Number of Refueling Stops
question: 'Minimum Refueling Stops' can be solved greedily using a max-heap. The greedy insight is:
options: A) Always refuel at the first available station
C) When stuck (can't reach next station), retroactively pick the largest refuel amount seen so far from the heap
D) Sort stations by fuel amount
explanation:
Use a max-heap of fuel amounts at passed stations. When current fuel can't reach the next station,
greedily pop the largest fuel from the heap (retroactively refueling there). Increment stops count. This greedy with
heap is O(n log n).

title: Generate Valid Parentheses — Counting
question: The number of valid parentheses strings with n pairs equals:
options: C) C(n) — the n-th Catalan number
explanation:
Valid parentheses strings with n pairs are counted by Catalan numbers: C(0)=1, C(1)=1, C(2)=2,
C(3)=5, C(4)=14. The backtracking generates all C(n) solutions.

title: Buying and Selling Stock — State Machine Summary
question:
Which state machine correctly models 'Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock III' (at most 2 transactions)?
buy1 = max(buy1, -price)
sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + price)
buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - price)
sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + price)
code: // States: buy1, sell1, buy2, sell2
options: A) Incorrect — should use 2D DP only
B) Correct — represents optimal profit at each stage of two transactions
C) Incorrect — buy2 should not depend on sell1
D) Correct only for unlimited transactions
explanation:
This elegant state machine captures two transaction stages. buy1: best profit if currently holding stock
from first buy. sell1: best profit after first sale. buy2: best profit after buying second stock (uses sell1 profit). sell2:
final profit after second sale.
COMPREHENSION

title: std::vector Capacity Doubling
question: After the following operations, what is the capacity of v?
explanation:
Starting at capacity 1: grows to 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 (after 16 pushes). The 17th push triggers another
doubling to 32. GCC/Clang typically use doubling; MSVC uses 1.5x growth. The capacity is 32.

title: std::vector vs std::deque Access Complexity
question: What is the complexity of random access by index for std::vector vs std::deque?
options: A) vector: O(1); deque: O(1) but with larger constant
explanation:
std::vector stores contiguous memory: O(1) by pointer arithmetic. std::deque uses chunked storage
(array of pointers to fixed-size blocks): O(1) mathematically (two-level index) but with larger constant due to
indirection.

title: Dangling Iterator After Reallocation
question: What happens to an iterator to a std::vector element after push_back causes reallocation?
options: B) Undefined behavior — iterator is invalidated if reallocation occurs
explanation:
If push_back triggers reallocation, all iterators, pointers, and references to vector elements are
invalidated. Dereferencing them is undefined behavior. Use index-based access to avoid this.

title: std::unordered_map Worst-Case Lookup
question: In the worst case (all keys hash to same bucket), std::unordered_map lookup is:
options: A) O(n) — degrades to linked list traversal
explanation:
std::unordered_map uses separate chaining. With all n keys in one bucket, lookup traverses the entire
chain: O(n). This occurs with hash collision attacks. Since C++11, some implementations switch to RB-tree (O(log
n)) when a bucket exceeds a threshold.

title: Smart Pointer — shared_ptr Reference Count
question: What does this code print?
explanation:
After make_shared and two copies, use_count=3. After p2.reset(), one reference dropped:
use_count=2. p1 and p3 still share ownership. Memory freed only when count reaches 0.

title: Move Semantics — std::move Effect
question: After std::move, what is the state of the moved-from object?
options: B) 0 or unspecified — s1 is in a valid but unspecified state
explanation:
After std::move, s1 is in a valid but unspecified state (standard guarantee). In practice, s1.size()
returns 0 (moved-from string is empty), but you should not rely on specific state. Accessing size() is safe; using
content is not.

title: RAII and Exception Safety
question: Why does using std::unique_ptr instead of raw new/delete guarantee no memory leak even with exceptions?
options: C) unique_ptr destructor runs during stack unwinding, freeing memory regardless of how scope is exited
explanation:
RAII: resource acquisition in constructor, release in destructor. When an exception unwinds the stack,
destructors of all local objects (including unique_ptr) are called in reverse order of construction, ensuring cleanup
regardless of exception.

title: Virtual Destructor Necessity
options: B) Undefined behavior — ~Derived() not called, causes memory leak
D) delete calls both destructors automatically
explanation:
Without virtual destructor, `delete b` calls Base::~Base() (static dispatch on Base*).
Derived::~Derived() is never called, so `data` array is never freed — memory leak and UB. Always declare base
class destructor virtual.

title: malloc vs calloc
question: What is the key behavioral difference between malloc and calloc?
options: B) malloc does not initialize memory; calloc zero-initializes the allocated memory
C) calloc takes one argument; malloc takes two
D) malloc is for single objects; calloc is for arrays
explanation:
malloc(n) allocates n bytes, content undefined. calloc(n, size) allocates n*size bytes AND
zero-initializes them. calloc(3,4) is conceptually equivalent to memset(malloc(12), 0, 12) but calloc may be
OS-optimized (requesting zeroed pages).

title: realloc Behavior on Failure
question: What is the bug in this realloc usage?
options: A) realloc should not be cast
B) If realloc fails and returns NULL, original pointer arr is overwritten with NULL, causing memory leak of original block
explanation:
If realloc returns NULL (allocation failure), assigning it to arr loses the only pointer to the original block
— memory leak. Correct pattern: `int* tmp = realloc(arr, 20*sizeof(int)); if (tmp) arr = tmp; else /* handle error, arr
still valid */`.

title: Struct Padding — Size Calculation
question: What is sizeof(S) on a 64-bit system with natural alignment?
explanation:
Layout: char a(1) + 3 padding + int b(4) = 8 bytes. Then char c(1) + 7 padding + double d(8) = 16
bytes. Total: 24. Struct padding aligns each member to its natural alignment and adds trailing padding to make
struct size a multiple of its largest member alignment (8).

title: Dangling Pointer — Use After Free
question: What is the output of this C program?
options: C) Undefined behavior — p is a dangling pointer after free
explanation:
After free(p), p points to deallocated memory — a dangling pointer. Dereferencing it is undefined
behavior. It may print 42 (value not yet overwritten), 0, garbage, or crash. Correct fix: p = NULL after free.

title: HashMap Treeification Threshold
question: In Java 8+, a HashMap bucket converts from a linked list to a Red-Black Tree when:
options: B) Bucket length exceeds 8 (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) AND total capacity >= 64
explanation:
HashMap.TREEIFY_THRESHOLD=8, MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY=64. When a bucket's chain
exceeds 8 entries AND the total table size is at least 64, the chain is converted to a TreeNode (RB-Tree). Below 64
total capacity, a resize is preferred instead.

title: String intern() and Memory
question: What does String.intern() return?
explanation:
b is an interned string from the string pool. a.intern() returns the canonical representation from the
pool — the same object as b. So b==c is true. a itself is a heap object (new String(...)), different from the pool
object: a==c is false.

title: GC Trigger During Deep Recursion
question:
A recursive algorithm allocating a new object at each call depth processes 10^6 levels. The JVM's primary
concern is:
options: B) StackOverflowError from exhausting the thread stack (each frame ~100-1000 bytes, default stack ~512KB-1MB)
explanation:
Default JVM thread stack is ~512KB-1MB. Each stack frame uses memory for local variables and
return addresses. At 10^6 levels, even 1 byte per frame overflows. This causes StackOverflowError (not
OutOfMemoryError). GC manages heap; the stack is separate.

title: ArrayList vs LinkedList — Cache Performance
question: For sequential iteration over 10^6 elements, ArrayList outperforms LinkedList primarily because:
options: A) ArrayList has O(1) size() method
B) ArrayList's contiguous memory layout is cache-friendly; LinkedList nodes are scattered in memory causing cache misses
explanation:
Modern CPUs prefetch cache lines (64 bytes) sequentially. ArrayList's backing array benefits from
spatial locality: iterating through it is cache-friendly. LinkedList nodes are heap-allocated individually with pointers
to next nodes — poor spatial locality causes frequent cache misses.

title: volatile vs synchronized
question: When should volatile be used instead of synchronized?
options: A) When multiple threads update a shared variable
B) When only one thread writes and others read a shared variable (visibility guarantee without atomicity overhead)
C) For compound operations like i++
D) volatile is always faster and should replace synchronized
explanation:
volatile guarantees visibility (writes are immediately flushed to main memory; reads bypass cache).
But it does NOT guarantee atomicity. i++ (read-modify-write) requires synchronized or AtomicInteger even with
volatile. Use volatile for simple flags written by one thread.

title: Java Memory Model — Object Creation on Heap
question: When `new MyObject()` is called in Java, the object is allocated:
options: A) On the stack if size < 64 bytes
B) On the heap (Eden space of Young Generation)
D) In the Old Generation immediately
explanation:
All Java objects are heap-allocated (unless JIT escape analysis proves they don't escape — 'stack
allocation' optimization). New objects go to Eden (Young Gen). Long-lived objects are promoted to Old Gen after
surviving several GC cycles.

title: std::map vs std::unordered_map — Ordered Iteration
question: Which statement correctly compares std::map and std::unordered_map?
options: A) unordered_map always has O(1) lookup
B) map: O(log n) all operations, keys sorted; unordered_map: O(1) average / O(n) worst-case, no order
explanation:
std::map is a Red-Black Tree: O(log n) for insert/find/erase, keys in sorted order, supports
lower_bound/upper_bound. std::unordered_map is a hash table: O(1) average, O(n) worst case, no ordering, no
lower_bound.

title: Pointer Arithmetic — Array Navigation
question: What does the following C code print?
explanation:
p = arr+2 points to arr[2]=30. *(p-1) = arr[1] = 20. *(p+1) = arr[3] = 40. Pointer arithmetic adds
multiples of sizeof(int) to the address, not 1 byte.

title: Rule of Three/Five/Zero
question: should also define:
code: C++'s 'Rule of Five' states that if a class defines any of {destructor, copy constructor, copy assignment}, it
options: B) Move constructor and move assignment operator (to avoid defaulted moves being incorrect or deleted)
explanation:
If you define a destructor (managing resources), the compiler-generated copy/move operations may
be wrong. Defining the destructor suppresses default move. The Rule of Five: always define all five (or none and
rely on Rule of Zero with RAII wrappers).

title: ConcurrentHashMap vs HashMap Thread Safety
question: ConcurrentHashMap in Java 8 achieves thread safety using:
options: A) Locking the entire map (like Hashtable)
B) Lock-free reads (volatile nodes) and CAS + synchronized on individual buckets for writes
C) ReadWriteLock on the whole map
D) Copying the map on each write (copy-on-write)
explanation:
Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap: reads are lock-free using volatile Node references. Writes use CAS for
empty buckets and synchronized on the head node of a bucket for non-empty ones. This allows maximum
concurrency without locking the whole map.

title: Function Pointer Syntax
code: Which declaration correctly declares a function pointer to a function taking int, returning double?
explanation:
Function pointer syntax: return_type (*pointer_name)(parameter_types). `double (*fp)(int)` declares fp
as a pointer to a function taking int and returning double. Option A declares a function (not pointer) returning
double*.

title: Lambda Capture — Reference vs Value
question: What does this code print?
explanation:
[&x;] captures x by reference. When f() is called, x is already 20. So f() returns 20*2 = 40. Contrast
with [x] (capture by value at lambda creation time), which would capture x=10 and return 20.

title: Integer Cache — == vs equals()
question: What does this print?
explanation:
Java caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127. a==b compares the same cached object: true.
128 is outside the cache range: c and d are distinct heap objects, so c==d compares references: false. Always use
.equals() for Integer comparison.

title: Template Instantiation — Code Bloat
code: A function template `template void sort(vector&)` instantiated with 10 different types generates:
options: A) One function shared by all types
B) 10 separate compiled functions (one per type) in the binary
explanation:
C++ templates are expanded at compile time. Each unique template instantiation (sort, sort, etc.)
generates separate machine code. This can cause 'code bloat' — binary size grows with the number of distinct
type instantiations.

title: Stack vs Heap — Return Address Safety
question: Why is returning a pointer to a local variable dangerous?
options: A) x is const and can't be pointed to
B) x is on the stack and is destroyed when getVal() returns; the pointer becomes dangling
C) This returns the address of x correctly
D) int* can't point to local variables
explanation:
Local variables live on the stack frame of their function. When getVal() returns, its stack frame is
reclaimed. The returned pointer now points to deallocated stack memory — undefined behavior when
dereferenced. Return heap-allocated memory or pass a pointer in as a parameter.

title: Stack Memory — Primitive vs Reference
code: In Java, when a method executes `int x = 5; String s = new String('hi');`, what is on the stack vs heap?
options: A) Both x and s are on the stack
B) x (primitive int, value 5) is on the stack; the String object is on the heap; s (reference) is on the stack
C) Both are on the heap
D) x is on the heap; s is on the stack
explanation:
Java: primitives and references are stored on the stack frame. The actual object a reference points to
is always on the heap. So x=5 (4 bytes on stack), s (reference/pointer, 4-8 bytes on stack), 'hi' String object (heap).

title: std::string SSO — Short String Optimization
question:
Most std::string implementations avoid heap allocation for short strings via SSO (Short String Optimization). The
typical threshold is:
options: C) 15-22 characters (implementation defined, typically 15 on GCC/Clang, 22 on MSVC)
explanation:
SSO stores short strings directly in the string object's internal buffer (using space that would
otherwise store pointer/size/capacity). GCC's libstdc++ uses 15 chars in-place; MSVC uses 15; libc++ uses 22.
This avoids heap allocation for common short strings.

title: sizeof Operator — Array Decay
question: What does this C code print?
options: C) 40 and 8 (on 64-bit — array decays to pointer when passed)
explanation:
sizeof(a) in main = 10 * sizeof(int) = 40. When passed to a function, arrays decay to pointers:
sizeof(arr) inside printSize = sizeof(int*) = 8 (64-bit). This is a classic C pitfall — always pass array size separately.

title: Garbage Collection — GC Roots
question: JVM GC roots include which of the following?
options: A) All objects in the Old Generation
B) Active thread stacks, static fields, JNI references, and class loader references
D) Objects in the Eden space only
explanation:
GC roots are starting points for reachability analysis. They include: local variables on thread stacks,
static fields of loaded classes, active JNI references, and references held by the JVM itself. Any object reachable
from a GC root is considered live.

title: Undefined Behavior — Signed Integer Overflow
code: In C++, what is the result of `int x = INT_MAX; x++;`?
options: B) Undefined behavior — signed integer overflow is UB in C++
explanation:
Unlike unsigned integers (which wrap around modulo 2^n, well-defined in C/C++), signed integer
overflow is explicitly undefined behavior. Compilers may assume it never happens and optimize accordingly,
producing surprising results if it does occur.

title: StringBuilder vs String Concatenation
question: In a loop concatenating n strings with +: `s = s + parts[i]`, the time complexity is:
options: C) O(n^2) — each + creates a new String object copying previous content
explanation:
String is immutable in Java. Each + creates a new String, copying all previous content. Concatenating
strings of total length L: total work is 1+2+3+...+L = O(L^2) = O(n^2) for n equal-length strings. Use StringBuilder
for O(n) concatenation.

title: Union Type Reinterpretation
question: What does this C code print on a little-endian system?
explanation:
On a little-endian system, the least significant byte is stored first. 0x01020304: byte 0 (c[0]) = 0x04 =
4, byte 1 = 0x03 = 3, byte 2 = 0x02 = 2, byte 3 (most significant) = 0x01 = 1. Answer: 4.

title: CRTP — Curiously Recurring Template Pattern
question:
CRTP is used to achieve:
template<typename Derived>
options: B) Static polymorphism — compile-time dispatch without vtable overhead
explanation:
CRTP achieves polymorphism resolved at compile time via static_cast, avoiding virtual dispatch
overhead (no vtable lookup). Useful for mixins and performance-critical code. The derived class type is known at
compile time via the template parameter.

title: finalize() vs try-with-resources
question: Why is try-with-resources preferred over finalize() for resource cleanup?
options: B) finalize() has non-deterministic timing (depends on GC), may never run, deprecated in Java 9+. try-with-resources guarantees immediate cleanup
explanation:
finalize() is called by GC — unpredictable timing, possibly never (app may exit), deprecated in Java 9,
removed in Java 18. try-with-resources (AutoCloseable.close()) runs deterministically at block exit, guaranteed for
resource cleanup.
